arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: The government argued that omitting an element is harmless. It cited a prior case involving jury instructions.
The defendant argued the Constitution mandates a single charging method. It stated that method is the federal indictment.
Justice Kennedy noted the lack of objection opportunities. He contrasted grand jury indictments with trial objections.
Justice Scalia asked if the Court must wait for a verdict. He questioned if the error is only clear after conviction.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: The case tests whether a federal indictment must list every offense element. The government claims a missing element is harmless if evidence proves guilt. The defendant claims the Constitution requires a complete indictment.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: The government wants the Court to affirm the conviction. It argues the missing element is harmless error.
The defendant wants the Court to reverse the conviction. It argues the missing element violates the Constitution.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: The government argues a missing indictment element is harmless. It cites precedent allowing harmless error in jury instructions.
The defendant argues the Constitution requires a complete indictment. It claims no other charging method exists.

sections.heading: What the justices asked
paragraphs: Justice Alito asked if the Court can answer the generic harmless error question. He questioned if the specific defect nature matters.
Chief Justice Roberts asked about probable cause timing. He wondered if prosecutors can indict before gathering all evidence.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: This case defines the minimum requirements for federal criminal indictments. It determines whether prosecutors can omit elements and rely on trial evidence. The outcome shapes the balance between prosecutorial discretion and defendant rights.
